analysis.one_liner: Tightens FAA oversight of aircraft makers after unsafe jets were certified with industry employees doing the government's checking.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on November 17, 2020 with no recorded opposition, but the Senate committee it was sent to never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rebuild the aircraft certification system that failed when two Boeing 737 MAX jets crashed, killing everyone aboard. Under the old system, the FAA delegated much of its safety-checking work to the manufacturers' own employees. The bill would require manufacturers to disclose safety-critical design information directly to the FAA, bar the FAA from delegating review of novel designs back to the maker, protect employees who report safety problems, penalize interference with the government's designated reviewers, and add money and staffing so FAA engineers can do the work themselves.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers and crews, who fly on planes whose safety-critical systems the FAA itself would review. Also aircraft workers, who would gain confidential, non-punitive safety reporting and stronger whistleblower protection, and FAA engineers and safety inspectors, who would get staffing money, retention incentives, and rules against interference with their oversight work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires aircraft manufacturers to adopt formal safety management systems that include a confidential, non-punitive employee reporting system and a code of ethics stating that safety is the organization's highest priority.

Requires manufacturers to disclose safety-critical information to the FAA — including any system that, without the flight crew's command, moves the aircraft — with civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per knowing violation and certificate revocation for individuals who knowingly make false statements.
Bars the FAA from delegating certification of a novel or unusual design feature to the manufacturer, and bars delegation made solely because the FAA lacks enough qualified staff.

Makes it unlawful for a manufacturer's personnel to interfere with the FAA-designated employees who perform certification functions, and prohibits manufacturers from restricting their employees' direct contact with the FAA.
Strengthens whistleblower protections to cover employees of manufacturers and their contractors who report aviation-safety violations, and protects them from retaliation.

Authorizes $27,000,000 per year for fiscal years 2021 through 2023 to recruit and retain FAA engineers, safety inspectors, human-factors specialists, and software and cybersecurity experts, and prohibits the FAA from paying its own staff more for hitting certification deadlines.

Imposes revolving-door restrictions: FAA supervisors may not oversee a certificate holder that employed them within the past year, and former FAA certification officials may not represent certificate holders before the agency for two years.
Requires new transport aircraft to account for realistic pilot response times in system design and to include flight-crew alerting systems that differentiate warnings, cautions, and advisories.

analysis.who_pays: Aircraft manufacturers, chiefly Boeing and the other companies holding delegation authorizations. They would bear compliance costs for mandatory safety management systems and new disclosures, exposure to civil penalties up to $1 million per violation, restrictions on the revolving door, and the loss of delegated self-certification for novel designs — costs that would slow certification and be passed to airline customers and ultimately ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Limiting the FAA's delegation authority and requiring expanded disclosure of safety-critical information would likely lengthen certification timelines and raise development costs for new aircraft — costs that manufacturers pass along to airlines and eventually to travelers.

The bill creates a formal appeal process that lets manufacturers escalate certification disputes up to the FAA Administrator, and it shields the final determination from judicial review — a new lever for companies contesting adverse certification decisions.
Many of its provisions are studies, expert panels, reviews, and reports rather than immediately binding standards, so the bill's effects would depend heavily on follow-through by the FAA.
The $27 million in annual staffing money is an authorization, not an appropriation — it is subject to Congress actually funding it, so the staffing expansion is not guaranteed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main provisions are a direct response to a real, documented breakdown: the FAA had delegated safety certification of new aircraft to the same companies being certified, and its own staff had their compensation tied in part to certification speed. The benefits — independent government review of safety-critical systems, protected reporting channels for workers, and penalties for concealment — address the specific pathway by which an unsafe automated flight-control design reached the flying public. The costs are real but ordinary: slower, more expensive certification of new aircraft, a compliance burden on manufacturers, and heavy reliance on studies and unfunded authorizations rather than immediate mandates. On balance the trade strongly favors travelers, and the design weaknesses are modest for a bill of this scope.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote with no recorded opposition, the Senate committee it was referred to never acted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 29, 2020 by Rep. Peter DeFazio and referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The committee discharged its Aviation subcommittee, marked the bill up the next day, and ordered it reported by voice vote; it was formally reported on November 16, 2020.
On November 17, 2020, the House passed the bill by voice vote under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, a fast-track method used for bills expected to face no opposition.
The Senate received the bill on November 18, 2020 and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had only three cosponsors — two House Republicans and one House Democrat — and no recorded opposition at any stage in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Aircraft manufacturers — above all Boeing and the other holders of FAA delegation authorizations — are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory safety management systems with confidential employee reporting, requirements to hand safety-critical design information to the FAA, civil penalties up to $1 million per violation, limits on delegated self-certification of novel designs, and new revolving-door restrictions. Air travelers and aviation workers, who would have gained the protections, got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The House passed the bill by voice vote with no recorded opposition and it carried cosponsors from both parties (2 Republicans and 1 Democrat); the Senate simply never voted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have ended much of the practice under which the FAA delegates certification of new aircraft to the manufacturers' own employees, forced disclosure of safety-critical design details (including flight-control software that moves the plane without pilot command), and imposed civil penalties up to $1 million per knowing violation. Manufacturers' interest in keeping delegated self-certification and confidentiality ran against passengers' interest in independent government review.

industries.industry: FAA technical workforce (engineers, safety inspectors, human-factors specialists)
industries.note: The bill authorized $27 million a year to recruit and retain technical staff, required retention incentives and training, banned pay adjustments tied to certification deadlines, and made it unlawful for manufacturer personnel to interfere with designated FAA unit members. Stronger, better-staffed independent oversight directly serves travelers.
Airlines would receive safer, better-reviewed aircraft and dedicated flight-crew alerting requirements, and held seats on the expert review panel; their direct costs under the bill were minimal.
